content.p: On the afternoon of 30 May 1925, police in the International Settlement of Shanghai fired into a crowd of Chinese students, workers and bystanders gathered outside a police station. The count of the dead is not agreed. One account, a history podcast, puts it at 12 killed and 17 injured; a British-side pamphlet says nine Chinese were killed and several wounded. The shooting set off a general stoppage by workers, shopkeepers and students in Shanghai, protests in cities from Hong Kong to Tientsin and up the Yangtse valley, and a year-long boycott of British trade in the south. It also led to two official inquiries, and the judges of the second could not agree on one report.
content.h2: A foreign-run city inside a Chinese one
content.p: Shanghai in 1925 was split into three areas: the Chinese-run old city, the French Concession and the International Settlement. The Settlement had grown out of the British and American concessions, and it stayed British-dominated, although other foreign powers took part in running it. According to the history podcast, about a million Chinese lived there by 1930 under a government run mainly by the British.

A writer in the American journal Foreign Affairs described the arrangement in October 1925. The Settlement held roughly a million people, of whom about 22,000 were foreigners. A Municipal Council of British, American and Japanese members, elected by foreign ratepayers, governed it. Three quarters of the population therefore paid taxes without a vote. An Advisory Committee of Chinese members had been set up only recently and, the writer said, its name showed how little power it had. Legal disputes went to the Mixed Court, which he called "Mixed" in name only because in practice foreigners controlled it.

The same writer was blunt about the cotton mills. He reported that skilled workers were paid 30 to 60 cents a day and unskilled workers from 7 to 50, that children between 10 and 14 worked twelve or fourteen hours a day, and that an anti-child-labour measure had been blocked at a ratepayers' meeting for lack of a quorum, the Japanese members having deliberately stayed away.
content.h2: The mill dispute and the arrests
content.p: Workers at Japanese-owned mills struck early in 1925. In May, according to the podcast account, the mill owners imposed lockouts at factories where workers resisted. In one of them workers broke in and wrecked the premises, and a Japanese guard opened fire and killed a worker. A British-side account, the Shameen pamphlet, tells the same event differently: a violent riot by mill hands, in which a Japanese overseer killed a Chinese workman. A mass meeting on 24 May founded an association to wipe out the disgrace of the killing.

Six students were then arrested in the Settlement. Two had collected money for the dead man's family and four had carried flags supporting the association. They were charged with disturbing the peace on 25 May and, the podcast says, were refused bail and held until 30 May so that the judge could consult a Japanese representative. Communists called for a mass demonstration outside their trial. Because protests were not allowed in the Settlement, small groups of students and workers slipped in and gathered outside the court. Foreign Affairs noted that during the trial of those arrested in the strike the court was guarded by armoured cars, machine guns and a cordon of Sikh police.
content.h2: The shooting at the police station
content.p: Scores of protesters were arrested at the court, the podcast says, so in the afternoon the demonstration moved to the police station where they were held. The police could not disperse the crowd and opened fire.

The fullest published picture of what happened at the station comes from questions asked in the House of Commons in July 1925, which cited evidence given in the Mixed Court. Two members of Parliament, Mr Adamson and Mr Scrymgeour, put it this way, and the Foreign Secretary did not confirm it, saying he had not yet received the court's report. Inspector Everson, who ordered the shooting, and other policemen were said to have admitted that he called out "Stop, stop!" in Chinese and English while holding up his pistol. Only a few of a crowd of about 2,000 students, workers and spectators could have heard or seen the warning, Adamson said, and shooting began ten seconds later. The questioners also said that live rounds, not blanks, were fired, that nobody aimed at legs, that the crowd was unarmed and trying to disperse, and that medical evidence showed some of the dead and injured had been shot from behind. Scrymgeour added that the students were six feet away when the police fired, that the order was given in English, and that more than 40 bullets were fired over several minutes.

The British-side account reads the same afternoon differently. It says a mob tried to rush the police station, which had been attacked and burnt by a mob in 1905, and that the police fired in its defence. That pamphlet, written from the British side, also claimed that Russian Bolsheviks took an active part in the disturbances. Foreign Affairs took the opposite view of responsibility: the Sikh policemen, its writer said, had merely switched on a mine that the Settlement's masters had long laid.

Shanghai answered with what the podcast calls a modified general strike, in which workers, students and merchants all stopped work. The Communist Party had founded the Shanghai General Labor Union in mid-May with Li Lisan at its head, and it took charge of the workers' side. A body called the Union of Labor, Commerce and Education led the movement and drew up 17 demands, ranging from the release of those arrested to the right to strike, freedom of speech and Chinese participation in governing the Settlement. It ran a newspaper, the Hot-Blooded Daily. The Shanghai Chamber of Commerce set up its own committee and put forward more moderate demands.

On 13 June the northern warlord's son Zhang Xueliang occupied the Chinese city. Some student leaders hoped he would help retake the Settlement. When they met him, the podcast says, he reminded them that he was there to restore order, and the labor union opposed their calls for an armed rising as doomed.

The strike wore down through the summer. The relief fund was paying 3 dollars per half-month by 20 July, down from 5 at the start; most of the money came from Chinese merchant associations and about 10 percent from the Soviet Union, the podcast says. Merchants backed out, classes ended, and on 7 July Li Lisan admitted that the union held about 100 strike-breakers prisoner. A settlement with the Japanese mill owners sent workers back on 21 August. The podcast judges it only slightly better than the one earlier in the year: a small contribution to a compensation fund and a promise not to dismiss workers without "just cause", which the owners themselves defined.

Its aftermath was harsh for union activists. The authorities closed the union's offices on 18 September and issued arrest warrants for Li Lisan and Liu Shaoqi, who both escaped the city. By the end of 1925, the podcast says, 2,700 union militants had been fired. Liu Hua, a worker from Sichuan and secretary of the West Shanghai Workers' Club, was arrested in November after the Settlement authorities found him in hospital, and was executed by a warlord who had pledged, in the British consul-general's words, to "suppress Bolshevism and disorder by the free use of the executioner's sword."

The movement spread south. According to the podcast, a protest of perhaps 100,000 people outside the British concession area in Guangzhou was fired on by British warships, killing more than 50. A strike and boycott centred on Guangzhou and Hong Kong lasted over a year, the podcast says, and 250,000 people left Hong Kong during it; the British government put three million pounds into the colony's economy.

The British-side Shameen pamphlet deals with a shooting at Shameen, Canton, on 23 June. It describes a commission appointed by the Canton government, whose report said British forces on Shameen suddenly opened fire on students crossing a bridge, used soft-nosed bullets and had been close to panic. The pamphlet's author rejected the commission's findings and called two documents attached to its report discredited. He dated the boycott from June 1925 to the autumn of 1926. This is one side's account of a disputed event, and the pamphlet itself is partisan.

Foreign diplomats in Peking set up two inquiries. The first was a diplomatic commission. In July 1925 the Foreign Secretary, Chamberlain, told Parliament that it had returned to Peking and that he would not yet publish its report. A member of Parliament, Mr Dalton, asked about strictures on the British chief of police, Mr MacEwan, but the answer did not address them.

The second was a judicial commission. A telegram from the American minister in China, preserved in the US Foreign Relations series, sets out its terms: American, British and Japanese jurists, with a Chinese jurist if the Chinese government named one, were to investigate the origin of the disturbances, the precautions taken to prevent them, the measures used to suppress them and the circumstances in which people died. Hearings were to be public and witnesses could be required to attend and give evidence on oath. The findings were to be unanimous if possible.

They were not. In February 1926 Chamberlain told the House that the three judges could not agree and that their separate reports went to the diplomatic body at Peking. The majority, he said, "completely exonerated the police". The Municipal Council nevertheless accepted the resignations of its Police Commissioner and of the inspector who gave the order to fire. It also expressed regret and tendered a cheque for 75,000 dollars to the senior consul for a compassionate grant to the wounded and the families of the dead. The Chinese authorities returned the cheque in early January, on instructions from the Ministry for Foreign Affairs, which said it had not been consulted. Documents on the incident and on the judicial commission were published in Peking on 23 December.
content.h2: The Mixed Court after the shooting
content.p: The Mixed Court itself became a point of dispute. Commissions of foreign ministers and of the Chinese foreign ministry began talks on 4 February 1926 about handing it back to Chinese control. In a dispatch to Washington, the American minister said they could not agree. He blamed the Chinese delegates for insisting on a purely Chinese court and vetoing foreign assessors in police and criminal cases, and he wrote that no handover could take place before the first anniversary of 30 May. He hoped the legations could take measures before then, to absolve themselves in public eyes of part of the blame, which he said should fall on the Chinese authorities. That was the American official view; the Chinese side's version is not in that dispatch.
